related_questions.question: How does a tax sale work in Pennsylvania?

text_blocks.snippet: In Pennsylvania, tax sales involve the sale of properties with delinquent property taxes. These sales occur through auctions, where the highest bidder wins the right to purchase the tax lien. The tax claim bureau in each county typically manages these auctions, which are announced publicly. Winning a tax lien means you're essentially buying the right to collect the overdue taxes, plus interest, from the property owner.
snippet_highlighted_words: involve the sale of properties with delinquent property taxes

list.snippet: This is the initial stage of the tax sale process.
Properties are offered for sale to satisfy the unpaid taxes.
If a property doesn't sell at the Upset Sale, it moves to the Judicial Sale.
This sale is a more formal process, often involving court involvement.
Properties sold at a Judicial Sale are generally free and clear of most liens and encumbrances, including those from the original sale.
In some cases, the original property owner or other interested parties may have the right to redeem the property after the sale.
This means they can pay off the outstanding taxes and reclaim ownership.
The specific redemption period (e.g., 9 months in some sheriff's sales) and procedures vary by county and sale type.
A tax lien is a legal claim against a property for unpaid taxes.
When you buy a tax lien, you're essentially stepping into the shoes of the taxing authority and have the right to collect the debt.
If the property owner doesn't pay the taxes and interest within a certain timeframe, the lien holder may be able to pursue foreclosure.
A tax deed is a legal document that transfers ownership of a property to the purchaser after a tax sale.
It is usually issued after a Judicial Sale or when the property is sold at a tax deed sale.

related_questions.question: How to buy a tax lien home in PA?

text_blocks.snippet: To buy tax lien properties in Pennsylvania, you'll need to participate in public auctions organized by county Tax Claim Bureaus. These auctions typically occur annually, with Upset Sales being the first opportunity to purchase properties with delinquent taxes. If properties remain unsold, they may be offered in subsequent Judicial or Repository Sales.
snippet_highlighted_words: participate in public auctions organized by county Tax Claim Bureaus

list.title: 1. Locate the County Tax Claim Bureau:
list.snippet: Each county in Pennsylvania has a Tax Claim Bureau responsible for managing delinquent taxes and tax sales. You can find contact information for your county's bureau on their official website.

list.title: 2. Research Properties and Attend Auctions:
list.snippet: County Tax Claim Bureaus advertise upcoming Upset Sales, often in local newspapers and on their websites. You'll need to research properties of interest and attend the auction to bid.
Upset Sale: This is the first sale of properties with delinquent taxes, typically for properties two years in arrears. Properties are sold subject to all existing liens and encumbrances.

Judicial Sale: If properties don't sell at the Upset Sale, they may be offered in a Judicial Sale. These sales may offer properties free and clear of some liens, but it's crucial to do your research as this isn't always the case.
Repository Sale: Properties remaining unsold after the Judicial Sale may be placed on a repository list for sale at a later date.

list.title: 4. Pre-registration and Fees:
list.snippet: Some counties require pre-registration with the Tax Claim Bureau and may charge a fee. For example, Erie County requires pre-registration at least 10 days before the sale and a $25 fee.

list.title: 5. Bidding and Payment:
list.snippet: At the auction, you'll bid on properties. If you win, you'll be responsible for paying the bid amount, plus any applicable transfer taxes, recording fees, and other costs.

list.title: 6. Due Diligence:
list.snippet: It's extremely important to conduct thorough due diligence on any property before bidding. This includes researching the property's history, existing liens, and any potential issues.

list.title: 7. No Guarantees:
list.snippet: Pennsylvania law generally states that properties are sold "as is," with no guarantee or warranty. You are responsible for any and all liens, encumbrances, and other issues associated with the property.

list.title: 8. Philadelphia Sheriff's Sales:
list.snippet: Philadelphia County conducts its tax sales through Bid4Assets.com, which requires online registration and a deposit.

list.title: 9. Municipality Approval:
list.snippet: In some cases, municipalities may have the right to deny a bid if a potential buyer doesn't meet their qualifications.

related_questions.question: What is the difference between a tax sale and a tax deed sale?
related_questions.snippet: There are two types of tax sales: a tax deed sale, which sells the property, including unpaid taxes, at auction; and a tax lien sale, which sells the liens on the property to a buyer who may then pursue the collection of monies owed.
